C0.quote: electoral competition between two non-ideological parties
C0.note: Game-theoretic analysis of a voting/power-sharing rule where voters can trade votes; strategic aspects of voting.

C1.quote: There exists a SPE where party platforms converge to the mid-range ideology.
C1.note: Existence and characterisation of subgame-perfect equilibria in the vote-trading and platform game.

C2.1.quote: Each voter has one vote and one unit of money.

C2.2.quote: individuals choose their vote-trading actions and to which party to designate
C2.2.note: Input is a vote offer (0/1) or monetary bid plus a party designation, not a ranking, approval set or score.

C2.3.note: Voters have ideal policies and utility functions.

C2.4.quote: individuals choose their vote-trading actions and to which party to designate
C2.4.note: Ideal policies and utilities are modelled separately from the vote-trading actions.

C3.1.quote: pure strategies that form a subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
C3.1.note: Voters choose bids, offers and vote designation strategically in every analysis.

C4.1.note: Input format is not RANK, WEAK, APPR, DICH or PAIR.

C5.1.note: Results concern equilibrium vote shares and platforms. Utilitarian and majoritarian comparisons appear only in the introduction (C9).

VOT.quote_behav: individuals choose their vote-trading actions and to which party to designate
VOT.note: Voters best-respond in the strategic market game.

CAN.quote_behav: Parties are non-ideological and aim at maximizing their vote shares.
CAN.note: Parties choose platforms strategically; they are proponents of policies.

C7.1.quote: pure strategies that form a subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
C7.1.note: Both voters and parties are strategic.

C8.1.quote: pure strategies that form a subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
C8.1.note: Second-stage subgames are solved by equilibrium, within the SPE.

C8.2.quote: pure strategies that form a subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)

claims.quote: vote markets are neither compatible with majoritarian principles
the insights provided by the analysis do not depend crucially
should continue to hold in alternative settings as well

C9.1.note: Claims about policy consequences of vote markets, their relation to majoritarian and utilitarian principles, and extension to other systems.

C9.2.note: Utilities, complete information, strategic behaviour and the power-sharing rule are all stated in the model. The extension claims are explicitly hedged.
